description: Driven by our love of space and the next frontier, our 6-member team—Josif Zoev, Renata Dacheva, Kostadin Proev, Darko Vasilev, Riste Endzekchev & Dimitar Kostadinov—unites science, engineering, and storytelling. NASA Space Apps 2nd Place, MASSUM 1st Place, and Junior Achievement 1st, 2nd & 3rd Place winners. We blend chemistry, robotics, electronics, PLCs, AutoCAD, AI, databases, 3D modeling, and media to build sustainable solutions for Earth and beyond.

Mars Material Legacy – From Mission Hardware to Future Mars Infrastructure

ASTROLABS developed a digital Material Passport information page using publicly available NASA data to help users explore the hardware left on and around Mars, discover its mission history, understand its original purpose, and learn about the scientific achievements it made possible.

Building on this educational foundation, we developed a concept for documenting and evaluating the potential reuse of selected materials from past missions. Our proposed Mars Reclaimer System (M.R.S.) works together with the Material Passport to record material origin, composition, condition, original function, potential applications, and required qualification tests.

As a practical application, we designed the concept of a modular Mars Legacy Air-Filter Cartridge and created a physical demonstration model to illustrate the idea. It is intended as a particulate pre-filter concept, not a replacement for certified life-support filtration systems.

Our project addresses the challenge by making Mars exploration hardware and its scientific legacy more accessible while extending the story toward sustainable future exploration. We believe that understanding what humanity has left behind can inspire the next generation and help us rethink how future missions use resources.
details:
Mars Material Legacy – From Mission Hardware to Future Mars Infrastructure

ASTROLABS began with a simple question: What has humanity left behind on Mars, and what can we learn from it?

Our project addresses NASA's "Abandoned but Not Forgotten" challenge through a digital educational platform that connects the history of Mars exploration with scientific discovery and future possibilities.

The Material Passport is designed as an accessible learning resource where visitors can explore Mars missions, discover the equipment left on and around the planet, understand its original purpose and learn about the scientific achievements it helped make possible. Its educational goal is to make the history of space exploration understandable and engaging, especially for school-age students and young people interested in science and technology. It encourages curiosity about Mars, introduces the importance of engineering and scientific research, and helps users understand that every mission leaves behind not only hardware, but also valuable knowledge.

The platform is functional and provides a foundation for further educational development. Future improvements could include more child-friendly explanations, interactive mission timelines, quizzes, challenges, visual storytelling and game-like activities that would encourage younger visitors to explore and learn.

We extended this idea through our proposed Mars Reclaimer System (M.R.S.), an intelligent material assessment and decision-support system. Its purpose is to determine whether a material from past mission hardware could have value for potential future reuse. Rather than assuming that every abandoned component should be recycled, M.R.S. evaluates relevant information such as material composition, condition, original function, possible contamination, safety requirements, potential applications and the testing needed before reuse.

Based on this assessment, materials can be classified into different decision categories: those that may be suitable for further qualification, those requiring additional investigation, and those that should be rejected for reuse. This approach helps avoid unsafe or inefficient recycling and ensures that material reuse is considered only when it is technically, environmentally and practically justified. The Material Passport provides the traceable record of each material, while M.R.S. supports the decision about what should happen next.

To demonstrate one possible future application, we designed *Astrofilter-X*, also known as the Mars Legacy Air-Filter Cartridge: a modular particulate pre-filter concept for future Mars habitat air-management systems. Our physical demonstration model uses a cardboard housing, textile layers, mesh, a computer cooling fan and Arduino electronics with sensors. It illustrates the proposed design, but it is not a tested filtration system and is not intended to replace certified HEPA or life-support filters.

Our development combined publicly available NASA mission data and historical documentation, digital research and web-based tools, visual design and presentation tools, and accessible electronic and physical components for the demonstration model.

What makes ASTROLABS creative is the connection between space education, historical storytelling, intelligent material assessment and sustainable engineering. We are not proposing to reuse everything left behind. We are proposing a responsible way to identify what may be useful, what needs further testing and what should never be reused.

Our intended impact is twofold: to make the legacy of Mars exploration more accessible to the next generation and to introduce a framework that could help future explorers evaluate selected mission materials as potential resources. We believe that understanding what humanity has left behind can inspire better decisions about what we take with us into the future.

Explore our work:
